text: As he left the office. <break time="0.8s" /> People crowded around him. <break time="0.8s" /> Asking questions. <break time="0.8s" /> With curious and mocking faces. <break time="0.8s" /> He told everyone about the string. <break time="0.8s" /> And even turned out his pockets. <break time="0.8s" /> But nobody believed him. <break time="0.8s" /> Get along, you old rascal. <break time="0.8s" /> They said, laughing. <break time="0.8s" /> And he grew angrier. <break time="0.8s" /> With every word they spoke. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening. <break time="0.8s" /> He walked home with three neighbors. <break time="0.8s" /> And showed them the place. <break time="0.8s" /> Where he had picked up the string. <break time="0.8s" /> The next day. <break time="0.8s" /> Around one oclock a farmhand named Marius Paumelle. <break time="0.8s" /> Returned the pocketbook to its owner. <break time="0.8s" /> He claimed. <break time="0.8s" /> He had found it on the road. <break time="0.8s" /> But not knowing how to read. <break time="0.8s" /> He had given it to his master. <break time="0.8s" /> When Hauchecorne heard the news. <break time="0.8s" /> He hurried around the village. <break time="0.8s" /> Telling his story again. <break time="0.8s" /> With its happy ending. <break time="0.8s" /> What hurt me. <break time="0.8s" /> Was not the thing itself. <break time="0.8s" /> But the lie. <break time="0.8s" /> He said. <break time="0.8s" /> For nothing hurts more than being called a liar. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet something still troubled him. <break time="0.8s" /> For people smiled at his story. <break time="0.8s" /> As if it were only a clever joke. <break time="0.8s" /> He felt that they were whispering behind his back. <break time="0.8s" /> But he could not understand. <break time="0.8s" /> Why they still doubted him.
